lede: Solid salt will not carry an electric current, but melt it and it will, and the current pulls the compound apart into its elements. That is electrolysis. This lesson follows the ions to the electrodes, names what forms at each one and what you see, and writes the reaction at each electrode.
can: Explain why a molten salt conducts and what electrolysis does to it.
Predict the product and the observation at each electrode for a molten salt.
Write the half equation at the anode and at the cathode (Higher).

text: A current that takes a salt apart

md: Push two graphite rods into solid lead(II) bromide, connect a d.c. supply, and nothing happens. Melt it and a current flows: a grey liquid gathers under one rod and red-brown gas bubbles from the other. The current is taking the compound apart.

md:
Follow the charges.
**Step 1, the ions.** PbBr₂ holds one Pb²⁺ ion for every two Br⁻ ions: +2 + 2 × (−1) = 0.
**Step 2, the pull.** Each Br⁻ ion carries a 1− charge, so it drifts to the **positive** rod, the **anode**. Opposite charges attract.
The negative rod is the **cathode**. PANIC checks it: Positive is Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

prompt: Molten lead(II) bromide is being electrolysed. Which rod do the positive lead ions move towards?
options: neither: they stay where they are
explain: Opposite charges attract. The negative Br⁻ ions drift to the positive rod, so the positive Pb²⁺ ions go the other way: to the negative rod, the cathode.

md: An ionic compound is built from **ions**. In the solid they are held in a lattice and cannot move. Melt it and the ions are **free to move**, so they **carry charge** through the liquid. So it must be **molten**, or dissolved.

title: Ions, not electrons
md: Electrons carry the current in the wires and the rods, but a molten salt has no free electrons. In the melt, **ions** carry the charge.

Follow one unit of PbBr₂ as it melts:
**Towards the cathode:** one Pb²⁺ ion carries +2.
**Towards the anode:** two Br⁻ ions carry 2 × (−1) = −2.
Both kinds of ion move, in opposite directions, carrying the charge across the liquid.

prompt: What carries the charge through molten lead(II) bromide?
explain: A molten salt has no free electrons: electrons move only in the wires and the rods. What moves through the liquid are the Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions, in opposite directions, and they carry the charge. The answer is ions.

md: In **electrolysis**, a direct electric current decomposes a liquid **electrolyte**: it breaks the compound down. The **electrolyte** is the molten or dissolved ionic compound: it **conducts** electricity **and is decomposed** by it. Each half of that sentence is a mark.

Test the definition on three liquids:
**Molten lead(II) bromide** conducts, and is decomposed: $\ce{PbBr2 -> Pb + Br2}$. An electrolyte.
**Molten lithium chloride** conducts, and is decomposed: $\ce{2LiCl -> 2Li + Cl2}$. An electrolyte.
**Mercury**, a liquid metal, conducts, but nothing is decomposed: it is still mercury afterwards. Not an electrolyte.

prompt: Complete the definition: an electrolyte conducts electricity and is ______ by it.
answer: decomposed | broken down | decomposed by it | decomposed by the current | decomposed by electricity | broken down by it | broken down by the current | split up | split up by it | broken up
explain: Conducting is only half of it: mercury conducts too, and it is not an electrolyte. An electrolyte is also broken down by the current, as lead(II) bromide becomes lead and bromine. The word is decomposed; in 2025 few candidates wrote it.

alt: One layer of graphite, carbon atoms joined in hexagons. One carbon is ringed with its three bonds drawn bold, and a dot beside it marks its fourth outer electron, which is delocalised and free to move along the layer.
caption: Graphite: each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one electron free to move.

md: The **anode** is the **positive** electrode and the **cathode** the **negative** one. An **inert electrode** takes no part in the reactions. Graphite is chosen for three reasons: it **conducts electricity**, it is **inert**, and it has a very **high melting point**.

Where the conducting comes from (C1):
**Step 1.** Each carbon atom has 4 outer electrons and bonds to 3 other carbons.
**Step 2.** That leaves 4 − 3 = 1 electron from each atom, **delocalised** and free to move along the layer. So graphite conducts **electricity**, not just heat.

prompt: An answer says graphite is used for electrodes because it is 'a good conductor'. Which two words must be added to earn the mark? (a good conductor of …)
explain: Graphite's delocalised electrons move and carry charge, so it conducts electricity. 'A good conductor' on its own could mean heat, and in 2023 examiners did not credit it. Write 'a good conductor of electricity'.

md: One sentence predicts every product: **opposite charges attract**. Metal ions are positive, so they go to the negative **cathode** and form the **metal**. Non-metal ions are negative, so they go to the positive **anode** and form the **non-metal**, as molecules: Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.

**Worked: molten calcium chloride, CaCl₂.**
**Step 1, the ions.** Calcium is in Group 2, so it loses 2 electrons: Ca²⁺. Chlorine is in Group 7, so it gains 8 − 7 = 1: Cl⁻.
**Step 2, the cathode (−).** Ca²⁺ is attracted there, so **calcium** forms.
**Step 3, the anode (+).** Cl⁻ is attracted there, so **chlorine**, Cl₂, forms.

prompt: Molten sodium bromide is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. Name the product formed at the cathode.
explain: Metal ions are positive, so they go to the negative cathode. Sodium ions, Na⁺, arrive there and become sodium atoms: the product is sodium.

prompt: Molten sodium bromide is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. Name the product formed at the anode.
answer: bromine | Br2 | Br₂ | bromine gas | bromine vapour | bromine (Br2)
explain: Non-metal ions are negative, so they go to the positive anode. Bromide ions, Br⁻, arrive there and join in pairs as Br₂: the product is bromine. Bromide is the ion you started with.

md: Examiners ask what you would **see**, not only what forms. Work it out from the product: is it a liquid or a gas in the hot melt, and what colour? Learn two colours: **chlorine is green**, **bromine is red-brown**. Both gases are **toxic**, so these cells are run **in a fume cupboard**.

**Lead(II) bromide, cathode.** The melt is at least 370 °C and lead melts at 327 °C: $370 > 327$, so lead forms as a **grey liquid**.
**Lithium chloride, anode.** Chlorine boils at −34 °C, far below the melt's 605 °C: $-34 < 605$, so it leaves as **bubbles of a green gas**.

prompt: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. What is seen at the anode?
explain: Bromine forms at the anode. It boils at 59 °C, so in the hot melt it is a gas, and its colour is red-brown: bubbles of a red-brown gas. The grey liquid is the lead, at the cathode.

prompt: Chlorine is toxic. Where must molten lithium chloride be electrolysed?
answer: fume cupboard | in a fume cupboard | a fume cupboard | in the fume cupboard | the fume cupboard | fume hood | a fume hood | in a fume hood | in the fume hood
explain: A toxic gas must be drawn away from the room, and that is the job of a fume cupboard. General advice such as 'wear goggles' does not earn this mark: name the fume cupboard.

caption: Electrons come down the wire into the cathode and leave the anode up the other wire.

md: A **half equation** shows the change at one electrode. At the cathode, ions **gain** electrons from the supply; at the anode, ions **lose** electrons to it. Write the ion and the product (a non-metal as its molecule), balance the atoms, then add electrons, e⁻, until the charges match.

**Cathode:** $\ce{Pb^{2+} -> Pb}$ has +2 on the left, 0 on the right. Two electrons on the left fix it: $\ce{Pb^{2+} + 2e^- -> Pb}$, and +2 − 2 = 0.
**Anode:** $\ce{2Br^- -> Br2}$ has −2 on the left, 0 on the right. Two electrons on the right fix it: $\ce{2Br^- -> Br2 + 2e^-}$, and 0 − 2 = −2.

prompt: In the anode half equation 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + ?e⁻, how many electrons are released?
explain: Balance the charge. The left side carries 2 × (−1) = −2 and the Cl₂ molecule carries 0, so electrons carrying −2 must go on the right: two of them. 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

prompt: Molten lithium chloride is electrolysed. Which is the half equation at the cathode?
explain: At the cathode the positive ion gains an electron from the supply, so the electron is written on the left with it. The charge is then +1 − 1 = 0 on the left and 0 on the right: Li⁺ + e⁻ → Li.

text: Higher: where the electron count comes from

md: Electrons are not added by guesswork. Charge is conserved, just as atoms are, so both sides of a half equation carry the same total charge. The number of electrons is the difference between the charge before and the charge after.

**Li⁺:** +1 before, 0 after: 1 − 0 = 1 electron gained, so $\ce{Li+ + e- -> Li}$.
**2Br⁻:** 2 × (−1) = −2 before, 0 after: 2 electrons lost, so $\ce{2Br- -> Br2 + 2e-}$.
The count always equals the charge on one ion times the number of ions.

prompt: A student writes Pb²⁺ + e⁻ → Pb for the cathode. Why does it lose the balancing mark?
options: the charges do not match: +1 on the left, 0 on the right
the electron belongs on the right
lead should be written as Pb₂
answer: the charges do not match: +1 on the left, 0 on the right
explain: Add up each side: +2 − 1 = +1 on the left and 0 on the right, so charge is not conserved. A 2+ ion needs two electrons, Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. The fault is that the charges do not match.

text: Higher: any molten halide, and aluminium oxide

md: The method works for any molten compound of a metal and a non-metal: CCEA can set halides you have not met, and the extraction of aluminium. Aluminium oxide holds Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Oxygen leaves as O₂, so two oxide ions meet at the anode, each carrying a 2− charge.

**Molten magnesium chloride.** Cathode: $\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e^- -> Mg}$. Anode: $\ce{2Cl^- -> Cl2 + 2e^-}$.
**Aluminium oxide, cathode.** $\ce{Al^{3+} + 3e^- -> Al}$: +3 − 3 = 0 on the left, 0 on the right.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Introducing Electrolysis"
why: A second walk through a molten ionic compound and its electrodes. If it goes on to solutions in water, that part is not on your specification.

prompt: At the anode in aluminium extraction, 2O²⁻ → O₂ + ?e⁻. How many electrons are released?
explain: Count the charge before: two oxide ions at −2 each make 2 × (−2) = −4. The O₂ molecule carries 0, so electrons carrying −4 go on the right: four of them.

text: Higher: reduction at cathode, oxidation at anode

md: The two half equations are the two halves of a redox reaction. **Reduction is the gain** of electrons, so the cathode reaction is always a reduction. **Oxidation is the loss** of electrons, so the anode reaction is always an oxidation: OIL RIG.

**Molten calcium bromide, cathode:** $\ce{Ca^{2+} + 2e^- -> Ca}$. The electrons are on the left, so 2 are gained: the Ca²⁺ ions are **reduced**.
**Anode:** $\ce{2Br^- -> Br2 + 2e^-}$. The electrons are on the right, so 2 are lost: the Br⁻ ions are **oxidised**.

prompt: At the cathode, Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. What happens to the lead ions?
options: they are reduced, because they gain electrons
they are oxidised, because they gain electrons
they are reduced, because they lose electrons
answer: they are reduced, because they gain electrons
explain: Look at where the electrons sit: on the left, with the Pb²⁺, so they are gained. Gaining electrons is reduction (OIL RIG), so the lead ions are reduced, because they gain electrons. The bromide ions at the anode are the ones oxidised.

text: See it done: a full Higher answer

md:
**The question.** Molten lithium bromide is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. Give the product, what is seen and the half equation at each electrode.
**Cathode (−):** lithium, a silvery-grey bead. $\ce{Li+ + e- -> Li}$: +1 − 1 = 0 on the left, 0 on the right.

**Anode (+):** bromine, bubbles of a red-brown gas. $\ce{2Br- -> Br2 + 2e-}$: −2 on the left, 0 − 2 = −2 on the right.
**Redox:** the bromide ions lose electrons, so they are oxidised; the lithium ions gain them and are reduced.
**Safety:** bromine is toxic, so the cell goes in a fume cupboard.

prompt: Molten potassium chloride is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. Which answer is right for the anode?
options: chlorine; bubbles of a green gas; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
chloride; bubbles of a green gas; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
chlorine; bubbles of a green gas; 2Cl⁻ + 2e⁻ → Cl₂
potassium; a grey liquid; K⁺ + e⁻ → K
answer: chlorine; bubbles of a green gas; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
explain: The negative chloride ions go to the positive anode, lose electrons and form the element, chlorine, which bubbles off as a green gas. Lost electrons sit on the right. So: chlorine; bubbles of a green gas; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

md:
**A colour names the gas.** A 2025 Higher question said only that a lithium halide gave a red-brown gas at the anode, and asked for its name. Work back from the colour:
**Red-brown** means bromine, $\ce{Br2}$, made by $\ce{2Br- -> Br2 + 2e-}$.
**The charges:** Li⁺ and Br⁻, +1 − 1 = 0, so the salt was LiBr, lithium bromide.

prompt: A green gas bubbles off the anode when a molten sodium halide is electrolysed. Which halide was it?
explain: Work back from the colour: green means chlorine, Cl₂, which forms from chloride ions. So the salt was sodium chloride. Red-brown would have meant bromine, and sodium bromide.

title: The electrode, not the terminal
md: In the 2025 Unit 7 paper, labels for the **anode** were often wrong: some pointed at the supply's terminal, some swapped the electrodes. The anode is the **rod** joined to the positive terminal, so put the label on the rod.

**Higher: a gas forms as molecules.** Oxygen, chlorine and bromine leave as two-atom molecules, and a half equation built on a lone atom loses every mark (2024 Higher). Start from the molecule: $\ce{O2}$ needs two oxide ions, so $\ce{2O^{2-} -> O2 + 4e^-}$, with 2 × (−2) = −4 on the left and 0 − 4 = −4 on the right.

prompt: (Higher) Fluorine, the first halogen, is made by electrolysing a molten fluoride. Which anode half equation earns all three marks?
explain: Fluorine, like the other halogens, leaves as a molecule, F₂, so start from two fluoride ions. They carry −2 and the molecule 0, and the electrons are lost, so they go on the right: 2F⁻ → F₂ + 2e⁻.

md: Each half equation also says how many electrons one atom of product costs. A lead ion needs two; a lithium ion needs one. So when the same number of electrons flows through two cells, they do not make the same number of atoms.

Send 6 electrons through each cell:
**Lead(II) bromide:** 6 ÷ 2 = 3 lead atoms.
**Lithium chloride:** 6 ÷ 1 = 6 lithium atoms.
**Aluminium oxide:** 6 ÷ 3 = 2 aluminium atoms.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Masses from a current and a time (Faraday's laws) and the electrolysis of solutions in water are not on your specification: molten salts only.

prompt: The same number of electrons flows through molten magnesium chloride and through molten sodium chloride. Which cell makes more atoms of metal?
options: sodium chloride, because each sodium ion needs only one electron
magnesium chloride, because a magnesium ion carries a bigger charge
neither: the same electrons make the same number of atoms
answer: sodium chloride, because each sodium ion needs only one electron
explain: Each atom of metal costs as many electrons as its ion's charge: two for Mg²⁺, one for Na⁺. So the same electrons make twice as many sodium atoms. Sodium chloride makes more, because each sodium ion needs only one electron.

md:
Explain why a molten ionic compound conducts: its ions are free to move and carry charge.
Define electrolysis, electrolyte, anode, cathode and inert electrode, and say why graphite is used.
Predict the product and what is seen at each electrode, and why a fume cupboard is needed.
Write both half equations for any molten halide and for aluminium oxide, and name the reduction and the oxidation (Higher).

Electrolysis usually fills most of one C2 question, often beside aluminium. Definitions are **[1]** to **[2]**: *decomposed*, *conducts*, positive anode, negative cathode. A product or an observation is **[1]** each: name bromine, not bromide, and give its colour and that it is a gas. A half equation is **[3]**: ion and product with an arrow, electrons on the correct side, then the balancing, each mark needing the one before.
